content: Non-specific cough is defined as a non-productive cough that occurs without any identifiable respiratory disease or known cause. This condition is commonly observed in children. Various treatments are used to manage this condition, including non-pharmacological approaches. Among these, air-modification interventions, such as ionisers, vaporisers, humidifiers, air filters, and regular vacuuming, have gained popularity and are part of a growing market. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of air-modification interventions in treating children with non-specific cough. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in several databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, OLDMEDLINE, and EMBASE. The most recent search was completed in November 2008. The inclusion criteria for this review required randomised controlled trials that compared air-modification interventions with placebo treatments, regardless of the duration of the intervention. The search results were assessed against these pre-determined criteria. Although five papers were initially considered for inclusion, none of them met the eligibility criteria. As a result, no data were available for analysis. The main finding of this review is that no randomised controlled trials have been conducted to evaluate the efficacy of air-modification interventions in managing prolonged, non-specific cough in children. Consequently, there is no evidence to support or refute the use of these interventions for this purpose. The authors concluded that, based on the currently available evidence, no recommendations can be made regarding the use of air-modification interventions for the treatment of prolonged, non-specific cough in children.
